original_question: For fixed d_1, ..., d_l with d_1 + ... + d_l = d and coprime bases q_1, ..., q_l, what are the optimal lower and upper metrical orders f(N) and g(N) for the discrepancy D_N of almost all finite-row Halton-Niederreiter sequences, with respect to a suitable measure, whose d_i-dimensional components are in base q_i?
target_in_paper: Section 2, Open Problem 6: the metrical discrepancy problem for almost all finite-row Halton-Niederreiter sequences.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the exact target as the finite-row version of the Halton-Niederreiter metrical discrepancy problem: it has the right dimension split d_1, ..., d_l with sum d, the right coprime base data q_1, ..., q_l, the right object (finite-row Halton-Niederreiter sequences), the right metrical flavor ('almost all' with respect to a measure), and the right goal of determining sharp lower and upper discrepancy orders for D_N.
missing_details: The paper's object is a Halton-Niederreiter sequence obtained by juxtaposing l digital sequences, where the i-th component is d_i-dimensional and in base q_i; this construction should be stated explicitly.
The bases should be stated as pairwise coprime, matching the paper's Halton/Halton-Niederreiter setup.
'Finite-row' must be defined: each row of each generating matrix of each digital component has only finitely many nonzero entries.
The paper does not take the measure as already fixed; it explicitly says that one first has to decide what a suitable measure on the class of finite-row Halton-Niederreiter sequences should be.

To match the paper's wording, the task is to determine the smallest possible upper-order function and the largest possible lower-order function for the discrepancy of almost all such sequences, not just 'optimal orders' in an unspecified sense.
To be stand-alone, D_N should be identified as the discrepancy of the first N points of the sequence; the paper uses discrepancy D_N here, not explicitly star discrepancy in Open Problem 6.
The scope should remain the finite-row subclass only; the paper treats the general Halton-Niederreiter problem separately as Open Problem 5.

The paper's nearby context adds motivation that the finite-row restriction is expected to lead to a smaller metrical discrepancy order than in the general case; this explains why Open Problem 6 is narrower than Open Problem 5.
If one wants the question to be fully faithful, it should not presuppose that the measure is already known; choosing/formulating it is part of the open problem itself.
refined_question: Fix positive integers d_1,\ldots,d_l with d_1+\cdots+d_l=d and pairwise coprime bases q_1,\ldots,q_l. Consider the class of d-dimensional Halton-Niederreiter sequences obtained by juxtaposing, for each i=1,\ldots,l, a d_i-dimensional digital sequence in base q_i; restrict to the finite-row subclass, meaning that every row of every generating matrix of every component sequence has only finitely many nonzero entries. After specifying a suitable probability measure on this class, determine as sharply as possible the metrical order of the discrepancy D_N of the first N points of almost all such finite-row Halton-Niederreiter sequences, i.e. determine the smallest possible upper-order function and the largest possible lower-order function for D_N for almost every sequence with respect to that measure.
justification: The draft is clearly aimed at Open Problem 6, not Open Problem 5, because it explicitly mentions finite-row Halton-Niederreiter sequences, almost-all behavior, and a suitable measure. The surrounding paragraphs in Section 2 define Halton-Niederreiter sequences as combinations of digital sequences of dimensions d_i in coprime bases q_i, define the finite-row restriction via the generating matrices, and stress that one must first decide on a suitable measure for these finite-row sequences. Open Problem 6 then asks for the sharp metrical discrepancy order for almost all such sequences. So the faithful refinement is to keep exactly that scope and make the hidden definitions explicit, without broadening beyond the finite-row case.
